claim: This study investigated the presence of the healthy vaccinee effect in two rigorously conducted COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness studies involving primary series and booster vaccinations.
source: This study investigated the presence of the healthy vaccinee effect—the imbalance in health status between vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals—in two rigorously conducted COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness studies involving primary series and booster vaccinations.

claim: Randomized controlled trials often have short follow-up durations, primarily involve healthy participants, and may cover only a limited range of clinical outcomes.
source: While randomized controlled trials (RCTs) remain the gold standard for determining vaccine efficacy, they often have short follow-up durations, primarily involve healthy participants, and may cover only a limited range of clinical outcomes (Janiaud et al., 2021; Nelson et al., 2009; Simonsen et al., 2007).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Real-world observational studies are frequently utilized to evaluate vaccine effectiveness beyond the controlled trial environment.
source: Real-world observational studies are frequently utilized to evaluate vaccine effectiveness beyond the controlled trial environment (Chambers, 2021; de Waure et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2009).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The indication effect occurs when individuals with underlying health conditions are more likely to receive vaccination, potentially leading to an underestimation of vaccine effectiveness.
source: The indication effect occurs when individuals with underlying health conditions are more likely to receive vaccination, potentially leading to an underestimation of vaccine effectiveness (Remschmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: The definition is provided with citation support.

claim: The healthy vaccinee effect occurs when healthier or health-conscious individuals are more likely to receive vaccination, leading to an overestimation of vaccine effectiveness.
source: Conversely, the healthy vaccinee effect occurs when healthier or health-conscious individuals are more likely to receive vaccination, leading to an overestimation of vaccine effectiveness (Remschmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: The definition is provided with citation support.

claim: Both indication effect and healthy vaccinee effect can bias and skew effectiveness results by conflating health status with the protective effects of the vaccine.
source: Both effects can bias and skew effectiveness results by conflating health status with the protective effects of the vaccine (Remschmidt et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2009).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Such effects have been documented in observational studies of influenza vaccine effectiveness.
source: Such effects have been documented in observational studies of influenza vaccine effectiveness (Remschmidt et al., 2015; Simonsen et al., 2005; Nelson et al., 2009; Jackson et al., 2006a), coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) vaccine effectiveness (Fürst et al., 2024; Høeg et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023), and prescriptive medication effectiveness (Nelson et al., 2009).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Such effects have been documented in observational studies of COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness.

evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Studies have documented a strong healthy vaccinee effect in estimations of influenza vaccine effectiveness among the elderly.

claim: Adjusting for coexisting conditions based on administrative healthcare utilization databases may not sufficiently control for the healthy vaccinee effect.
source: While it is common for studies to control for such effect by adjusting for coexisting conditions based on administrative healthcare utilization databases, this approach may not sufficiently or properly adjust for this effect, as it may not capture the illness severity, recency, duration, or the functional status of individuals—factors that can confound the association between vaccination and health outcomes, particularly in the elderly (Jackson et al., 2006a; Remschmidt et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2009).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The healthy vaccinee effect is potentially strongly time dependent, most pronounced immediately after vaccination but gradually diminishing.

claim: Seriously ill individuals, those with deteriorating health, and frail, less mobile elderly persons are less likely to be vaccinated, resulting in a higher short-term mortality risk among the unvaccinated.
